newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech economic ship showing signs of taking on water.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech economic ship showing signs of taking on water.

text.p: The often-praised Czech economy may be starting to show cracks from the pressure of an economic slowdown, a rising trade deficit and problems in the capital market that continue to drive investors away.

Over the years, economists have hailed Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his policies which have produced one of the lowest inflation rates in the region, good GDP growth and an unemployment rate of about three percent.

Many of those same analysts are now saying that while the economy is not yet in serious trouble, it is showing signs of wear and tear brought about by inefficiencies and shortfalls in its restructuring.
"For all the Thatcherite rhetoric, the Klaus government has not exposed the economy to unfettered market forces," Merrill Lynch said in a September investor report.
"Compared to other Central European nations, the Czech Republic has proved dilatory in restructuring enterprises in order to improve efficiency," the report added.

Two years ago, Klaus boated that while some ex-communist neighbours were trying to avoid drastic economic surgery, the Czech Republic was already out of the operating theatre and in the fitness centre, building up muscle.
Since 1992 the economy has moved from recession to 4.8 percent consumption-driven real growth in 1995, as inflation fell from double digits to below nine percent.
Unemployment remains around three percent, and official statistics say nearly 70 percent of the economy is made by companies in, at least nominally, private hands.
Czechs, for the most part, are fully employed, buying truckloads of western goods, and living in incredibly cheap state-controlled housing.
ANALYSTS WARNINGS
But analysts, following the Klaus analogy, say there are signs the patient may have fooled the doctor into thinking its wounds had healed.

Last week the Czech Statistical Bureau released figures showing gross domestic product growth slowed in the second quarter, sending some disappointed analysts scrambling to revise their full year forecasts downward.
Real economic growth for the second quarter slowed to 4.0 percent year-on-year from 4.6 percent in the first quarter.

"The preliminary GDP growth (of 4.0 percent) as reported for the second quarter by the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) last week was significantly lower than we expected," said Martin Kupka of Patria Finance.
This week Patria revised its full year GDP forecast downward by one percentage point to 4.5 percent, while the CSU forecast remains at 5.1 percent.
GOVERNMENT SHOULD DO MORE TO BOOST EXPORTS

Analysts say responsibility for the downturn could be be attributed partly to the sluggish performance of many of the Czech Republic's major trading partners in the European Union and some said the government should do more to boost exports.
Despite signs the climb in imports is levelling out, the rapidly-growing trade deficit continues to spook many analysts and is at the heart of a troubling current account deficit.

The first half current account deficit widened to $1.7 billion from $722.5 million in first half of 1995. In rapidly increasing numbers, Czechs are buying foreign goods for their factories and also their garages and living rooms.
The trade deficit ballooned to a record 100.9 billion Czech crowns ($3.74 billion) for the January-August period, up from 59.5 billion for the same period last year.

Klaus, who has said until now that the trade deficit merely reflected the cost of a necessary modernisation of Czech industry, has called a meeting of ministers and officials on October 8 to tackle the problem.

Meanwhile, the capital account surplus -- which had previously covered a huge inflow of imports during the Czech economic transformation -- plummeted in the first half to $800.8 million from $3.1 billion for the period last year.

Josef Poeschl, a Czech specialist at the Vienna Institute for Comparative Economic Studies (WIIW), says a huge jump in the current account deficit beyond 1995's four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) could seriously damage confidence.

"The government has two alternatives: to accept a devaluation which I do not think would be a catastrophe. The other choice concerns the trade deficit, where they could slow imports by implementing an import surcharge," he said.
"If the current account deficit gets to be around six or seven percent of GDP, it can be dangerous."

Merrill Lynch said: "Exports need to be stimulated if the foundations for stable and sustained growth are to be established, and if the currency is to be preserved at current levels over the longer term."
STABLE CROWN CORNERSTONE OF ECONOMIC REFORM
A stable crown has been one of the cornerstones of Klaus's economic reforms.

This has made the crown a target for speculators who have found the combination of stability and real interest rate differentials against western currencies of around seven percent irresistable, pushing it to record highs.

That stability may be in jeopardy, with analysts pointing to a recent banking crisis that has exposed problems in capital market regulation, and weakened the crown by some three percent against the dollar in less than a week.
In August, the Czech National Bank rescinded Kreditni Banka's licence after it ran up losses estimated at nearly 12 billion crowns following a series of non-performing loans and debt swaps.
Later it put Agrobanka, the fifth largest Czech bank, under forced administration, saying it had become illiquid partly due to its ties to Kreditni and investment group Motoinvest.
Investors have long complained about transparency problems in the Czech markets, with many choosing the smaller Polish and Hungarian markets where legislation is more developed.
"Clearly there are problems in the Czech banking system," said Jan Vanous, director of economic analysis firm PlanEcon.

"It's a problem of what I would call morally unsuitable investors from Czech financial institutions that should never have been allowed to either set up a bank, or become a major shareholder in one," he said, without naming names.

Vanous said the current system, set up in large part by Klaus as finance minister in the former Czechoslovakia, has created a circle of ownership that is stalling badly-needed restructuring at many firms and is hindering economic output.
"We have a set-up where the state controls the banks, the banks control the investment companies, and investment companies control the enterprises -- It's one cosy set up.

"What we need is to achieve some clear separation from the state, particularly the financial sector, and then put pressure on the banks to make money instead of being instruments of state policy. This would do a lot to help repair the economy." ($1=26.96 Czech Crown)
